question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Slightly ______ bitter oranges to remove the red color which covers their skins.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. grate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a verb in the imperative form that means to rub food against a rough surface so as to shred it. "Grate" is exactly that verb — one grates the peel (skin) of oranges to take off the outer red/orange layer. (कद्दूकस करना)

◦ Correct: Slightly grate bitter oranges to remove the red color which covers their skins.

• The sentence is a recipe-style instruction, so a bare imperative verb ("grate") is required, not a noun or an adjective.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "great" is an adjective meaning very good/large — it cannot act as the verb of the sentence.

• Option 3 "grace" as a verb means to honour or adorn something; it does not mean to scrape off a skin.

• Option 4 "grade" means to arrange or rank in grades/classes — again it does not fit "to remove the red color".

NOTE

• Watch out for such homophone-like confusables in SSC papers: grate (to shred / a fireplace frame) vs great (excellent), grate on (to irritate). Related kitchen verbs: grate, peel, mince, chop, dice, whisk.

question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pausity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pausity" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "Paucity", which means scarcity; the presence of something in only very small quantities. (कमी / अल्पता)

◦ Example: There is a paucity of reliable data on rural employment.

• Spelling key: PAU + CI + TY (the sound is /s/ but the letter is c, as in "paucity", "scarcity", "capacity").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Phlegmatic" (correct) — having an unemotional, calm and stolidly composed temperament. (शांत स्वभाव वाला)

• "Philistine" (correct) — a person who is hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts. (कलाविमुख व्यक्ति)

• "Philanthropy" (correct) — the desire to promote the welfare of others, expressed especially by generous donation of money. (परोपकार)

NOTE

• Words from the Greek root phil- ("love"): philanthropy (love of mankind), philosophy (love of wisdom), bibliophile (lover of books), philology (love of words/language).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Wealthy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Affluent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Wealthy" means having a great deal of money, property or possessions; rich. Its closest synonym among the options is "affluent", which also means rich and prosperous. (धनी / समृद्ध)

◦ Example: They live in an affluent (wealthy) neighbourhood of the city.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Depressed" means sad/dejected (or, of an area, suffering economic hardship) — it is not a synonym of wealthy.

• Option 3 "Lacking" means deficient or missing something — the opposite idea.

• Option 4 "Poor" is the direct antonym of wealthy.

NOTE

• Synonyms of wealthy: affluent, prosperous, well-off, well-heeled, opulent, moneyed.

• Antonyms of wealthy: poor, needy, destitute, impoverished, penniless, indigent.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

A calculated move to gain an advantage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gambit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "gambit" is a device, action or opening remark that is calculated to gain an advantage. The word comes from chess, where a gambit is an opening in which a player sacrifices a pawn to gain a positional advantage. (सोची-समझी चाल)

◦ Example: Offering a discount was a clever gambit to attract new customers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Grunt" — a low, short guttural sound made by an animal or a person. (घुरघुराना)

• Option 2 "Bonsai" — the Japanese art of growing ornamental, artificially dwarfed trees in pots.

• Option 4 "Profit" — financial gain; the difference between the amount earned and the amount spent. It is a result, not a calculated move.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often asked in SSC: stratagem/ploy (a cunning plan), ruse (a trick to deceive), manoeuvre (a skilful movement or plan), gambit (an opening move made to gain an advantage).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

If the dog (is allow complete freedom), it can assume that any toy is acceptable for play.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. is allowed complete freedom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The clause needs the passive voice: "is + past participle (V3)". The past participle of "allow" is "allowed", so the correct structure is "is allowed complete freedom".

◦ Correct: If the dog is allowed complete freedom, it can assume that any toy is acceptable for play.

• The subject "the dog" is singular, so the auxiliary must be "is", not "are".

• "Complete" is an adjective and correctly modifies the noun "freedom".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "allowed completely freedom" — the adverb "completely" cannot modify the noun "freedom"; it also drops the auxiliary "is".

• Option 3 "No substitution required" is wrong because "is allow" is ungrammatical (auxiliary + base form is not a valid passive).

• Option 4 "are allowed complete free" — wrong number ("are" with the singular "dog") and "free" (adjective) is used where the noun "freedom" is needed.

NOTE

• Passive voice pattern: object + be (am/is/are/was/were) + V3 (+ by agent). Example: The rules are enforced strictly. Always check (i) subject–verb agreement and (ii) that the main verb is in the third form.

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

Social media is ______ to market products.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. used.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• After the auxiliary "is", a past participle (V3) is required to form the passive voice. The V3 of "use" is "used".

◦ Correct: Social media is used to market products.

• The sense is passive: social media is not doing the using — it is the thing that is used (by people/companies) in order to market products.

• "to market products" is an infinitive of purpose ("in order to market products"), which fits neatly after the passive verb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "uses" — "is uses" is ungrammatical (two finite verbs together).

• Option 3 "use" — "is use" is not a valid structure; the base form cannot follow "is".

• Option 4 "using" would make it active continuous ("is using"), which would wrongly suggest that social media itself is marketing products, and it also leaves the sentence without an object.

NOTE

• Structures after be: be + V3 = passive (is written); be + V4/-ing = continuous (is writing). Also learn the fixed pattern "be used to + noun/-ing" (be accustomed to) vs "used to + V1" (past habit).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

What customs officials are asking for are not things that _______ their own personal titles.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. aggrandize.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Aggrandize" means to increase the power, status, wealth or reputation of someone; to enhance or make greater. Things that "aggrandize their own personal titles" are things that add to their personal standing. (बढ़ाना / महिमामंडित करना)

◦ Correct: ... are not things that aggrandize their own personal titles.

• The blank needs a transitive verb that can take "their own personal titles" as its object — only "aggrandize" and "advocate" are transitive here, and only "aggrandize" gives the required sense of enlarging one's status.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "accede" means to agree to a demand or to take up an office; it is intransitive and takes "to" (accede to a request).

• Option 3 "acerbic" is an adjective (sharp and forthright in tone), so it cannot be the verb of the clause.

• Option 4 "advocate" means to publicly recommend or support; one does not "advocate a title".

NOTE

• Word family: aggrandize (verb), aggrandizement (noun — "self-aggrandizement" means the act of increasing one's own power or importance). Synonyms: magnify, exalt, enhance, elevate. Antonyms: belittle, diminish, demean.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Forciing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Forciing" is incorrectly spelt. The correct spelling is "Forcing" — the present participle of the verb "force" (to compel somebody to do something). (मजबूर करना)

◦ Spelling rule: when a verb ends in a silent -e, the -e is dropped before adding -ing: force → forcing, make → making, write → writing, come → coming.

• The extra "i" in "forciing" makes it wrong; there is never a double "i" in such forms.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "Trust" (correct) — firm belief in the reliability or truth of someone/something. (विश्वास)

• "Shopping" (correct) — here the final consonant is doubled because "shop" is a short verb ending in a single vowel + single consonant: shop → shopping (also stop → stopping, run → running).

• "Wave" (correct) — a moving ridge of water; to move the hand to and fro.

NOTE

• Three key -ing rules: (i) drop silent -e (hope → hoping); (ii) double the final consonant after a short stressed vowel (begin → beginning); (iii) -ie changes to -y (die → dying, lie → lying).

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

It's good to travel and / work, most beautiful than going / to the same office each day.
option_3: to the same office each day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. work, most beautiful than going.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "than" signals a comparison between two things, and a comparison always takes the comparative degree, never the superlative. Hence "most beautiful than" is wrong; it must be "more beautiful than".

◦ Correct: It's good to travel and work, more beautiful than going to the same office each day.

• "Beautiful" is a long adjective (3 syllables), so its comparative is formed with "more" and its superlative with "the most".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Segment "It's good to travel and" is correct — "It is good to + V1" is a standard structure.

• Segment "to the same office each day." is correct — "each day" is a proper adverbial of frequency.

• Because a definite error exists, "No error" cannot be the answer.

NOTE

• Degrees of comparison: beautiful – more beautiful – most beautiful; good – better – best; bad – worse – worst. Rule: use the comparative with "than" and the superlative with "the" / "of all" / "in the class". Never write "more better" or "most beautiful than".

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

It would be neat and / cleanest, a home worthy of / spending our lives together.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. cleanest, a home worthy of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The two adjectives joined by "and" must be in the same degree (parallel structure). The first is "neat" — a positive degree adjective — so the second must also be positive: "clean", not the superlative "cleanest".

◦ Correct: It would be neat and clean, a home worthy of spending our lives together.

• A superlative such as "cleanest" also needs a group to compare within (e.g., "the cleanest house in the town"), which is absent here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Segment "It would be neat and" is correct — "would be" expresses a hypothetical/future-in-the-past idea.

• Segment "spending our lives together." is correct — "worthy of + V-ing" is the standard pattern (worthy of praise / worthy of spending).

• Since a clear error exists, "No error" is not the answer.

NOTE

• Parallelism is a favourite SSC topic: items joined by and/or/but must share the same grammatical form — "neat and clean", "reading and writing", "not only fast but also accurate".

question:
Select the word from the options which is similar in meaning to the bracketed word given in the sentence below.

There is widespread (prejudice) against workers over 45.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Intolerance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Prejudice" means a preconceived opinion or unfair bias against a person or group that is not based on reason or actual experience. The closest option is "intolerance" — an unwillingness to accept views, beliefs or people different from one's own. (पूर्वाग्रह / असहिष्णुता)

◦ Correct sense: There is widespread intolerance (prejudice) against workers over 45.

• The phrase "prejudice against" clearly indicates hostility/bias, which "intolerance" captures.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Concern" means worry or interest — it is neutral and far weaker than prejudice.

• Option 3 "Temperament" means a person's nature or disposition.

• Option 4 "Misfortune" means bad luck.

NOTE

• Synonyms of prejudice: bias, partiality, bigotry, intolerance, preconception, discrimination.

• Antonyms of prejudice: impartiality, fairness, open-mindedness, tolerance. Note the related word prejudicial (harmful to someone's interests).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

Can we reschedule the meeting? I ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. have a headache.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• With ailments the standard collocation in English is "have + a/an + illness": have a headache, have a cold, have a fever, have a toothache. The speaker is describing a condition happening now, so the simple present "I have a headache" is right. (मुझे सिरदर्द है)

◦ Correct: Can we reschedule the meeting? I have a headache.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "take a headache" is not an English collocation — we take medicine, a rest or a break, not a headache.

• Option 3 "get a headache" means the headache starts/develops (a repeated or future event, e.g., "I get a headache whenever I read in the dark"); it does not state a present condition.

• Option 4 "give a headache" would mean causing someone else pain ("This noise gives me a headache").

NOTE

• Useful health collocations: have a cough/cold/fever/sore throat; catch a cold; suffer from asthma; come down with the flu; take medicine; feel dizzy.

question:
Select the word from the options which is exactly opposite in meaning to the bracketed word given in the sentence below.

She relished our (arguments), most of which she won.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. agreements.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Arguments" here means heated disagreements or verbal disputes. Its exact antonym is "agreements" — situations of harmony and shared opinion. (तर्क-वितर्क / झगड़े का विलोम — सहमति)

◦ Contrast: They had frequent arguments, but finally reached several agreements.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "feud" — a long-running bitter quarrel: a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 2 "negotiations" — discussions aimed at reaching a deal; a process, not the opposite of a quarrel.

• Option 4 "altercation" — a noisy quarrel: again a synonym of argument.

NOTE

• Synonyms of argument (quarrel sense): dispute, altercation, squabble, row, feud, wrangle.

• Antonyms: agreement, accord, concord, consensus, harmony. (Note that "argument" can also mean a reason put forward in support of an idea.)

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bracketed idiom in the given sentence.

He is (a wolf in sheep's clothing), outwardly kind but inwardly vicious!
option_3: A situation involving a narrow escape from danger
option_4: Angry today about something that occurred in the past
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A dangerous person pretending harmless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a wolf in sheep's clothing" means a dangerous or harmful person who pretends to be gentle and harmless. The rest of the sentence — "outwardly kind but inwardly vicious" — explains the idiom exactly. (भेड़ की खाल में भेड़िया)

◦ Example: Beware of that broker; he is a wolf in sheep's clothing.

• The expression comes from Aesop's fable and also from a Biblical warning about false prophets.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes the idiom "to tear someone off a strip / haul over the coals" (to scold).

• Option 3 describes "a close shave / a narrow escape".

• Option 4 describes holding "a grudge" or "raking up the past".

NOTE

• Related idioms of deceit: "cry wolf" (raise a false alarm), "crocodile tears" (insincere sorrow), "snake in the grass" (a treacherous person), "two-faced" (hypocritical).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

We was installing wood flooring throughout our house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. installed wood.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "We" is plural, so the singular auxiliary "was" is wrong; "was installing" cannot go with "we" (it would have to be "were installing"). The sentence simply reports a completed past action, so the simple past "installed" is the best correction.

◦ Correct: We installed wood flooring throughout our house.

• "Wood flooring" is a standard noun + noun compound (like "wood panelling", "stone flooring"), so "wood" need not become "wooden".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "No improvement" is wrong because "We was" violates subject–verb agreement.

• Option 3 "installs wood" is the singular present form and does not agree with "We" (we install / he installs).

• Option 4 "installs wooden" repeats that agreement error and needlessly changes the compound noun.

NOTE

• Subject–verb agreement with "be": I was; he/she/it was; we/you/they were. In the present: I am, he/she/it is, we/you/they are. Use the simple past for a finished action with no continuing sense.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

I had been angry the whole / evening, so she rubs brahmi / oil into my scalp to cool my brain.
option_1: oil into my scalp to cool my brain.
option_4: I had been angry the whole
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. evening, so she rubs brahmi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The first clause is in the past perfect continuous/past tense ("I had been angry the whole evening"), so the verb in the following clause must also be in the past. The present tense "rubs" breaks this sequence of tenses; it should be "rubbed".

◦ Correct: I had been angry the whole evening, so she rubbed brahmi oil into my scalp to cool my brain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Segment "I had been angry the whole" is correct — "had been + adjective" with a duration ("the whole evening") is fine.

• Segment "oil into my scalp to cool my brain." is correct — "rub something into" is the right collocation and "to cool" is an infinitive of purpose.

• As a definite tense error exists, "No error" is not the answer.

NOTE

• Rule of sequence of tenses: if the principal clause is in a past tense, the subordinate clause is normally also in a past tense (He said that he was ill). Exception: universal truths stay in the present (He said that the sun rises in the east).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

In fits and starts
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Irregularly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "in fits and starts" means irregularly; with many stops and starts; not steadily or continuously. (रुक-रुक कर)

◦ Example: The old engine ran in fits and starts all the way home.

◦ Example: He studies in fits and starts, which is why his marks fluctuate.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Be in difficulty" is the sense of idioms like "in hot water" or "in a fix".

• Option 3 "Everywhere" corresponds to "far and wide" or "high and low".

• Option 4 "Summary" corresponds to "in a nutshell" or "in brief".

NOTE

• Similar idioms of manner: "by fits and starts" (same meaning), "off and on / on and off" (occasionally), "now and then" (sometimes), "round the clock" (continuously — the opposite idea).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.

Plain
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Fancy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As an adjective, "plain" means simple, undecorated, without any ornament or elaboration. Its antonym is "fancy", meaning elaborate, decorated or ornamental. (सादा का विलोम — सजावटी / भड़कीला)

◦ Contrast: She wore a plain cotton saree, not a fancy silk one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Stupid" (foolish) is unrelated — the opposite of "clever", not of "plain".

• Option 3 "Crazy" (mad) is not the opposite of plain.

• Option 4 "Mean" (unkind or stingy) is the opposite of "generous/kind".

NOTE

• "Plain" has several senses: simple/undecorated (opposite: fancy, ornate); clear and easy to understand (opposite: obscure); frank ("plain speaking"); and as a noun, a large flat stretch of land (e.g., the Northern Plains).

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

Urging or requesting (someone) solemnly or earnestly to do something
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Adjure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Adjure" means to urge or request someone solemnly or earnestly to do something, often as though under oath. (सत्यनिष्ठा से आग्रह करना)

◦ Example: The judge adjured the witness to tell the whole truth.

• It is the only verb among the options; the other three are nouns, so they cannot express an action of urging.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Arrears" — money that is owed and should have been paid earlier. (बकाया)

• Option 3 "Armada" — a fleet of warships (famously the Spanish Armada of 1588).

• Option 4 "Arena" — a level area surrounded by seating, used for sports or entertainment.

NOTE

• Similar verbs: implore/beseech (to beg earnestly), exhort (to strongly encourage), entreat (to ask earnestly), enjoin (to instruct or urge to do something). Note also the word family: adjure (verb) → adjuration (noun).

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

How (can a book such as) be written before I'd lived the incidents it described?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. could such a book.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word order is "such a + noun" (determiner + article + noun), so it must be "such a book", not "a book such as". "Such as" is used only when examples follow (e.g., "fruits such as mangoes").

◦ Correct: How could such a book be written before I'd lived the incidents it described?

• The rest of the sentence is in the past ("before I'd lived"), so the past modal "could" agrees with the tense far better than the present "can".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No correction required" is wrong because "a book such as be written" is ungrammatical.

• Option 3 "must so a book" is meaningless — "so" cannot replace "such" before a noun.

• Option 4 "may such a book" has the right word order but the wrong modal: "may" expresses permission/possibility in the present, clashing with the past-perfect "I'd lived".

NOTE

• such vs so: use "such + (a/an) + adjective + noun" (such a good film) and "so + adjective/adverb" (so good, so quickly). Modal pairs: can → could, will → would, may → might, shall → should.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

At the core of the (1) ______ lies the fierce (2) ______ between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. The lifelong struggle (3) ______ the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur culminates (4) ______ bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which (5) ______ kings of that period participated and perished.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. epic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes the Mahabharata — the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and the battle of Kurukshetra. The Mahabharata is an "epic", i.e., a long narrative poem about heroic deeds. So "At the core of the epic lies the fierce rivalry ..." is the natural reading. (महाकाव्य)

◦ Correct: At the core of the epic lies the fierce rivalry between two branches of the Kuru dynasty ...

• The blank follows "the", so a noun is required, and "epic" is the only option that works as a noun here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "dull" and 3 "bright" are adjectives and give no sense after "the core of the ...".

• Option 2 "exercise" is a noun but is contextually absurd — an exercise has no "fierce rivalry between two branches of a dynasty" at its core.

NOTE

• "Epic" as an adjective means heroic or grand in scale ("an epic journey"). The two great Indian epics are the Ramayana and the Mahabharata; the Mahabharata, attributed to Ved Vyasa, is the longest epic poem in the world.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

At the core of the (1) ______ lies the fierce (2) ______ between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. The lifelong struggle (3) ______ the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur culminates (4) ______ bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which (5) ______ kings of that period participated and perished.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. rivalry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank sits between the adjective "fierce" and the phrase "between two branches of the Kuru dynasty", so it needs a noun denoting competition or enmity. "Rivalry" means a state of intense competition or hostility between people or groups. (प्रतिद्वंद्विता)

◦ Correct: ... lies the fierce rivalry between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas.

• "Fierce rivalry" is also a very common collocation in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "commute" means to travel regularly between home and work — completely out of context.

• Option 3 "hostile" is an adjective (unfriendly); the noun form "hostility" would have fitted, but the adjective cannot follow "the fierce".

• Option 4 "friendship" contradicts "fierce" and the whole idea of a lifelong struggle.

NOTE

• Synonyms of rivalry: competition, contention, opposition, antagonism, feud. Antonyms: cooperation, friendship, alliance, harmony.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

At the core of the (1) ______ lies the fierce (2) ______ between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. The lifelong struggle (3) ______ the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur culminates (4) ______ bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which (5) ______ kings of that period participated and perished.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. between.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The struggle is between two identifiable sides — the Pandavas and the Kauravas, described as "the cousins" (the two branches of the Kuru dynasty). For two parties, English uses the preposition "between". (के बीच)

◦ Correct: The lifelong struggle between the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur ...

• Also, "struggle/conflict/war between X and Y" is the standard collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "amongst" (a variant of "among") is used for more than two, or for an undivided group — here only two rival branches are meant.

• Option 2 "inside" refers to position within an enclosure, not to a relationship.

• Option 4 "along" means beside/following the length of something.

NOTE

• Preposition rule: between = two persons/things clearly distinguished ("between you and me"); among/amongst = more than two, or a mass ("share it among the five of you"). "Between" is also acceptable for more than two when each item is considered individually (e.g., treaties between the four states).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

At the core of the (1) ______ lies the fierce (2) ______ between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. The lifelong struggle (3) ______ the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur culminates (4) ______ bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which (5) ______ kings of that period participated and perished.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. in the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "culminate" takes the preposition "in" — to culminate in something means to reach its final and highest point in that thing. The following noun phrase "bloody battle of Kurukshetra" is a specific, uniquely identified battle, so it needs the definite article "the". Hence "in the bloody battle of Kurukshetra". (परिणत होना)

◦ Correct: ... culminates in the bloody battle of Kurukshetra ...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "in that" would need a clause after it, not a noun phrase.

• Option 2 "inside" wrongly suggests physical location and drops the required article.

• Option 4 "in to" is a wrong split; "into" (one word) shows movement, and "culminate into" is not standard English.

NOTE

• Verb + preposition combinations frequently tested: culminate in, result in, consist of, comprise (no preposition), insist on, object to, depend on, deprive of. Use "the" before unique or already-specified nouns (the battle of Kurukshetra, the Ganga, the Sun).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

At the core of the (1) ______ lies the fierce (2) ______ between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. The lifelong struggle (3) ______ the cousins for the throne of Hastinapur culminates (4) ______ bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which (5) ______ kings of that period participated and perished.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. most.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed directly by the plural countable noun "kings", so it needs a quantifier meaning "the greater part of". "Most kings of that period participated and perished" is the correct and idiomatic reading. (अधिकांश)

◦ Correct: ... the bloody battle of Kurukshetra, in which most kings of that period participated and perished.

• "Most + plural noun + plural verb (participated)" agrees perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "total" is an adjective/noun used with amounts ("the total number of kings"), not directly as a quantifier before a plural noun in this sense.

• Option 2 "almost" is an adverb and cannot modify a noun on its own; it would have to be "almost all kings".

• Option 4 "each" takes a singular noun and a singular verb ("each king participates"), which clashes with "kings ... participated".

NOTE

• Quantifier rules: most/many/few/several + plural noun; much/little + uncountable noun; each/every + singular countable noun. "Almost" must be paired with all/every/no ("almost all", "almost every", "almost no").
